card.hook: Get here early and you might have the whole street to yourself, with a little tiled-roof bridge sitting at the end of it like it's waiting for you. By the evening, you'll be sharing it with half of Hoi An.
card.stand_here: Stand on Nguyễn Thị Minh Khai, at the western end of the street. The bridge is a very short step east of there, at the far end of the street, so face east and look straight along it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so the street and the bridge both fit. Then try 2x or higher (depends on your phone) to bring the bridge closer. Use 0.5x only if you want lots of street in front, and keep the bridge in the middle so its sides don't stretch.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the bridge's centre on the middle vertical line, and tap the bridge, then drag the slider to make it a little darker so the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Go before about 6:30am, when a local guide says the street is usually almost empty. Crowds build from about 19:00, and the bridge is often full of people in the evening, so evening shots may include a lot of people.
card.selfie_here: Try the spacious waterside pavement in front of the bridge, by the Hoai River. A travel guide names it as one of the best picture spots, and says the bridge is lit at night. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and keep the bridge over your shoulder, but check your framing on the spot.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on the south bank of the canal and shoot toward the bridge, with the lanterns in the background.
card.rules_and_safety: Photographing the outside is free, but crossing the bridge or entering the temple needs the Hoi An Ancient Town ticket, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Line the bridge up on the middle gridline, then see if you can get one shot of that long street with nobody in it.
card.good_to_know: The bridge is about 18 metres long and 3 metres wide. Japanese merchants began building it in 1593 and finished in 1595, and a temple was added on top in 1653. It's been repaired several times since, so you'll spot Japanese, Vietnamese and Chinese details.

card.hook: Stand in the middle of a bridge as the light fades and Hoi An's Old Town rooftops line up across the water, with the lanterns starting to glow in the river. It's a bit like watching a town switch itself on.
card.stand_here: Walk onto Cầu An Hội and go to the middle of the span. Face the Old Town, so its roofs and skyline sit across the water in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole skyline and its reflections. Then try 1x for a cleaner, less stretched look at the roofs. Zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) is good for picking out a lantern or a single boat on the far bank.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest lantern or the bright part of the sky, then slide it a little darker so the lights keep their colour instead of turning white.
card.best_time: Aim for about 5:00 to 6:30 PM, and arrive a little before the light starts to go. Take a few shots while the sky is bright, then more as the lanterns come on. Sunset time changes with the season, so check it for your date.
card.selfie_here: Head to the Thu Bon riverside walkway on Bach Dang Street in the Ancient Town and put the water directly behind you. At sunset the river turns pink-gold, so your front-camera selfie picks up the sky. Try zoom 0.5x to fit more of the scene behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on An Hoi islet (cross Cầu An Hội from the Old Town) while you stand on the Old Town bank across the water, and check it works when you get there.
card.rules_and_safety: Check the current situation on the bridge when you arrive. At night, hold the phone with both hands or brace your elbows on the railing so the shot stays sharp.
card.challenge: Get the far bank on the upper third gridline, then catch at least one lantern reflected in the water below it. Bonus points if the rooftops don't slope.
card.good_to_know: The Thu Bồn is the river Hoi An's Old Town looks out over. Guides often call Cầu An Hội one of the best sunset spots on the river, with the widest view of the Old Town. If you want boats in the shot, Cầu Cẩm Nam shows fishing boats and lantern boats. Cầu Cửa Đại is further out at the river mouth, so treat it as a separate outing.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk onto Cầu An Hội and go to the middle of the span. Face the Old Town, so its roofs and skyline sit across the water in front of you.

card.hook: Two dragons, a tiled roof and two sides that match almost perfectly: the outer gate of the Fujian Assembly Hall is the one bit of Hoi An that rewards you for being a bit fussy about where you stand. Guides call it the hall's favourite photo spot.
card.stand_here: Stand on Trần Phú Street, right in front of the outer gate (the tam quan). The phone icon on the map is at the gate itself, so there's no extra walk. Face the gate squarely from the middle.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the straight-on shot. If you can't fit the whole roof in from the street, tap 0.5x. Then try 2x or higher for close-ups of the dragon ornaments.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines, line the roof up with a horizontal line and keep the phone level so both sides match and the roofline stays straight.
card.best_time: Early or late in the day is likely to be quieter. Crowds vary, so give it a minute and wait for a gap in the people walking through the entrance.
card.selfie_here: Head into the first courtyard, go to the upper level and stand in front of the Three-arched (Triple) Gate so it fills the background. Use the front camera and tap 0.5x if your phone offers it, so the gate stays over your shoulder. For a second option, go to the lower level, on the left, by the flower-shaped pond with the five-carp statue.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Trần Phú Street pavement facing the outer gate, while you stand right in front of the gate, so they can fit the whole gate and roof behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are generally fine in the courtyards and outdoor areas, but be discreet inside the main hall, especially during ceremonies. Avoid flash near altars, and don't stand in front of anyone who is praying or bowing. Floors can be slippery, so wear shoes with grip. One source warns that Trần Phú Street can flood between October and December.
card.challenge: Take one dead-straight, perfectly symmetrical shot of the gate, then one with you in the middle. Which dragon looks smugger?
card.good_to_know: The Fujian Assembly Hall (Hội quán Phúc Kiến) is a Chinese assembly hall in Hoi An's Ancient Town. Past the outer gate, the courtyard has a porcelain-inlaid triple gate with a yin-yang tile roof and coiling dragons. It's not confirmed whether the courtyard needs a separate ticket, since the Ancient Town ticket may apply, so check when you arrive.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Trần Phú Street, right in front of the outer gate (the tam quan). The phone icon on the map is at the gate itself, so there's no extra walk. Face the gate squarely from the middle.

card.hook: You step in from the bright street and your phone blinks for a second in the dim rooms, just like your eyes do. That's your cue: Tan Ky House is a spot for small frames, not big views.
card.stand_here: Stand right at Tan Ky House, where the phone icon on the map sits. The house is the subject, so use the doorway or the front of the building and shuffle a step or two sideways to find the cleanest angle.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the front of the house and the doorways. Inside, switch to zoom 0.5x if a room is too tight, and keep the phone level so the walls don't lean. Use zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for details up high that you can't get close to.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the part of the scene you care about, then slide it a little darker if a bright doorway looks washed out.
card.best_time: Go earlier in the day when it's quieter and the light outside is softer. It's dim indoors at any hour, so hold the phone with both hands and tuck your elbows in.
card.selfie_here: Head to the yellow back wall on Bach Dang Street, on the riverside, on the other side of the house from the Nguyen Thai Hoc entrance. Visitors love it for photos, especially in ao dai, and it gets good light at sunrise and sunset. Use the front camera at arm's length and check on the spot whether the house itself shows up behind you. At the front facade at 101 Nguyen Thai Hoc Street, the yellow walls, dark wood shutters and lantern hooks make a nice backdrop too.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are allowed inside, but skip the flash to protect the antiques, and follow any signs or staff instructions. In the late afternoon, look carefully before crossing the road, because lots of cyclos move through there.
card.challenge: Find a doorway with bright light behind it and line it up with the gridlines so it stands perfectly straight.
card.good_to_know: Tan Ky House is a historic house in Hoi An with National Heritage status. The interior and the character of the building are both worth a look. It may be ticketed or have visiting rules, so check the official site before you go.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at Tan Ky House, where the phone icon on the map sits. The house is the subject, so use the doorway or the front of the building and shuffle a step or two sideways to find the cleanest angle.
